Toward 23-25 (Monster/Red Bull level) over a couple of years
One year after the prior Stifel appearance, management reinforced a strongly bullish narrative; distribution points roughly doubled since the October 1, 2022 Pepsi switch.

The Pepsi transition was 'as smooth as anyone can recall' - ~80% of distributors moved on October 1 as a 'one light switch,' helped by 60-90 day termination clauses, partner buyouts, and hiring ex-Pepsi reps.
The biggest surprise was the rapid success in food service (~10% of Pepsi revenue) after only three or four months - unusual for an energy brand.
ACV at 95% was achieved 18-24 months ahead of internal plans.
Sales velocity (repeat purchase) is growing strong double digits on a two-year accelerating basis despite the distribution doubling - suggesting accelerating underlying demand.
Management acknowledged quarter-end inventory 'inconsistencies' (a Q4 2022 pullback and ~$20M of excess Q1 2023 order timing) and committed to disclosing them each quarter.
~68% of consumption is incremental (24% new-to-category, 44% user intensification); the 24% new-to-category figure is called the 'silver bullet' for long-term growth.
Celsius averages ~14 SKUs per location vs 23-25 for Monster/Red Bull; closing that gap and building double/triple facings for a 'billboard effect' will take a couple of years.
Convenience is the 'last frontier' Celsius just entered and remains 'in its infancy' (entered only 7-8 of Circle K's 13 divisions last year) - a multi-year growth lever.
Management positions Celsius as a total-beverage opportunity as usage occasions expand beyond traditional energy.
The US is the priority for capital given known ROI; international expansion will be methodical, 'no spray and pray,' leveraging Pepsi bottlers (Britvic/Centauri in the UK, Asahi in Australia).
The powder business has grown exponentially at Walmart and Target; on-the-go sticks are seen as a sizable future adjacency.
The summer is the first peak season at full 95% ACV - a large '100 days of summer' display-activation program runs with Pepsi frontline reps.
Retailers are reallocating shelf space to energy from declining categories (CSDs, teas, cold coffee) and seeking incremental dollar rings as tobacco consumption declines.
Adjacent-category opportunities, including white space in the Pepsi portfolio, are on the three-to-five-year roadmap, but timing, sequencing and core-portfolio focus come first.
What surprised management about the unusually smooth Pepsi distribution transition, and where does the opportunity go from here?

John Fieldly attributed the smooth transition to extensive preparation, treating legacy AB partners well (buyouts, upfront communication), 60-90 day termination clauses letting ~80% transition on October 1, and hiring ex-Pepsi reps; significant optimization remains. Toby David: the biggest surprise was rapid food-service success (~10% of Pepsi revenue), with Pepsi providing a platform into restaurants, fast casual, colleges, hospitals, hotels and vending. Hitting 95% ACV 18-24 months ahead of plan was also unexpected.
Are channel inventories correctly positioned heading into summer, and is more sell-in needed so retailers do not run out given sales trends?

John Fieldly: Celsius has full visibility into Pepsi mixing-center inventory and believes it is well positioned; the company is keeping its own inventory up entering the '100 days of summer.' He noted a Q4 2022 pullback and ~$20M of excess Q1 2023 order timing, committed to disclosing such inconsistencies each quarter, and pointed analysts to scan data as the truer demand indicator.
Distribution roughly doubled since October but Celsius is still ~20-30% below Bang's peak and ~50% of Monster - what is the right level of distribution points?

John Fieldly declined a target, saying Celsius is 'just getting started,' focused on velocity and optimizing existing distribution with secondary/third placements and branded coolers. Toby David: Celsius averages ~14 SKUs per location vs 23-25 for Monster/Red Bull and aspires to climb to those levels and build double/triple facings for a 'billboard effect' - but that will take a couple of years.
Facings in high-share markets vs national
How do total facings in high-share markets like South Florida compare to the national average, and is that a reasonable level to reach over time?

Toby David: replicating high-share-market facings is the aspiration; South Florida is the strongest at ~22% share vs ~8 nationally, with Miami still under-indexed; Celsius also over-indexes in Southern California, Dallas and New England; replicating the South Florida playbook in the 23 newly expanded markets would be a 'home run.'
How does management think about the overall level of doors and placements for energy as a category, and the opportunity for second/third energy coolers per store?

John Fieldly: management's view has broadened from going after the energy category to going after total beverage as usage occasions expand; retailers are adding doors and expanding energy planograms in recent resets while reducing CSDs, teas and cold coffee, because energy provides incremental dollar rings as tobacco and other categories decline.
How does management quantify Celsius's overall incrementality and how does it aid category expansion?

Toby David: per numerator, 24% of Celsius consumers are new to category and ~44% are user intensification, totaling ~68% incremental; the 24% new-to-category figure is the 'silver bullet' - compounding younger, new-to-category consumers and retaining them is how Celsius can become the first #3 brand to genuinely challenge the two big players.
70% of Monster/Red Bull sales come from convenience vs ~56% for Celsius (up from 51-52% pre-Pepsi) - how does the mix evolve and what is the opportunity?

John Fieldly: convenience was the 'last frontier' and Celsius is now there, with the #2 Amazon position (~19% share) validating demand; the better-for-you, functional and fitness trends drive velocity; management would intuitively expect ~70% convenience mix, but the food-service opportunity could change the mix and make the overall opportunity larger.
Why has sales velocity not decelerated even though distribution points have doubled (with a gentle note that conference samples were free)?

Toby David: velocity is growing strong double digits on a two-year accelerating basis despite the distribution doubling. John Fieldly noted the concurrent untracked club-channel launch would intuitively have offset velocity but the brand is still working. David attributed sustained velocity to low household penetration and tactical reinvestment in historically under-exposed markets (Midwest, Pacific Northwest), with more capital deployed than ever.
Does the convenience channel - single-serve cold packs at the highest ring - help velocities as the convenience share expands toward Monster/Red Bull levels?

John Fieldly: convenience is the highest-turn segment Celsius just entered, so it absolutely should help. Toby David: Celsius is 'brand new' in convenience (entered 7-8 of Circle K's 13 divisions for the first time last year) and remains 'in its infancy,' so the 56% revenue figure leaves a massive opportunity. Fieldly cited the successful 7-Eleven green apple cherry launch as validation.
Who is the core Celsius consumer, where does brand awareness stand and how is it accelerated, and how does it compare to Monster and Red Bull?

John Fieldly: the consumer base is ~52% male / 48% female, inclusive, targeted at 18-24 with a fruit-forward, non-aggressive positioning; the gym/pre-workout DNA helped post-COVID. Toby David: the brand historically skewed 25-45 but has aged down while retaining older consumers, many of whom do not self-identify as energy-drink users. Broad appeal is attributed to the sustained-energy experience (no spike and crash).
How does management think about US brand awareness as a stepping stone to an international discussion?

John Fieldly: US household penetration is low single digits per the last data poll; Celsius started with five 'drill deep' markets and scaled them annually as distribution expanded, with 2024 plans to expand further; the US is critical to global success and shows the best returns on investment.
How does management think about brand awareness and strategy for international markets?

John Fieldly: the US must be won first, with international foundational seeds built on top; Celsius already has presence in Sweden (~10 share), Finland, the Baltics, Puerto Rico and parts of Asia. Toby David: international expansion will be strategic and methodical - 'no shocking approach' - targeting the largest international energy markets and leveraging Pepsi bottlers (Britvic/Centauri in the UK, Asahi in Australia), but the US remains the focus because every international dollar takes longer to return.
Confirming media/advertising spend at ~20-22% of sales as the right go-forward level - how does management think about properties, sponsorships, athletes and events, and US vs international spend?

John Fieldly: there are international properties with global acceptance - Formula 1 (dominated by Red Bull) being an example, with Celsius partnered with Ferrari for the US races; social media's global connectivity means influencers carry some global awareness, and authenticity and local insights will be a competitive advantage when launching new markets.
How does management think about using innovation to expand usage occasions and extend the growth runway, as Monster has done?

John Fieldly: the current focus is flavor innovation (Fantasy Vibe, Oasis Vibe launched at Coachella), with more flavors in 2024; adjacent-category opportunities exist including white space in the Pepsi portfolio, but timing and sequencing across three-to-five-year plans are key with the core portfolio the priority; the powder business has grown exponentially and on-the-go sticks are a sizable future adjacency.
